papers.title: The Great Game: A Model of Geoeconomic Competition
papers.abstract: We build a model of two hegemons that have valuable trading relationships with each other and at the same time compete in exerting geoeconomic power over countries in the rest of the world. When the hegemons trade with each other, their optimal policy is shaped both by classic economic considerations - the profitability of that specific trade - and by geoeconomic competition - how the trade affects the power of each hegemon vis-a-vis the rest of the world. We show that containment, a policy mix in which a hegemon limits sales of its inputs to the rival hegemon and uses its power to demand that the rest of the world shift away from sourcing from the rival, arises when the two hegemons offer relatively substitutable exports, are less interdependent with each other, and have more direct geopolitical rivalry. Countries in the rest of the world benefit, all else equal, from hegemons containing each other since they partially squander their power with offsetting demands. However, containment policy can also worsen the efficiency of global production, leaving the rest of the world worse off.

papers.title: Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand
papers.abstract: How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures? Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market. As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers. Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month. Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs. First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers’ capabilities have expanded. Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products. Third, switching rises around major model releases. Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure. Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes. Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers’ pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services.

papers.title: When Cash Wakes Up: Inertia in Institutional Money Market Funds and the Potential Effects of AI Disruption
papers.abstract: We study institutional cash management by constructing a novel dataset that records the specific money market funds (MMFs) held by each mutual fund in each month from 2010 to 2024. We document remarkably high inertia: more than half of mutual funds never switched their MMF choice throughout the sample period, despite non-negligible yield dispersion. To decompose the sources of this inertia, we develop a two-stage structural model that separately identifies the determinants of portfolio managers’ attentiveness (“waking up”) and their conditional preferences once attentive. We estimate the model using a methodology that combines BLP-style contraction mapping with maximum likelihood. We establish three main findings. First, MMFs with less attentive investor bases engage in greater liquidity transformation while offering lower yields. As a result, they earn higher profits and exhibit significantly higher survival rates, especially during periods of low interest rates. Second, we find that aggregate flows appear more yield-sensitive during low interest rate periods (the well-documented “reaching for yield” phenomenon) not because individual investors become more yield-seeking, but because a larger fraction of investors becomes attentive—a composition effect rather than a preference shift. Third, counterfactual analysis reveals a potential tension between market efficiency and financial stability if AI-driven automation reduces investor inattention. In the absence of inattention, fees fall by approximately half, yield dispersion collapses to near zero, and market concentration declines by roughly 20%, but monthly fund flows increase by about three times and the incidence of fund-months in which redemptions exceed a fund’s weekly liquid assets rises by about six times, raising the risk of fire sales and MMF runs.

papers.title: Coasian Stakeholder Theory
papers.abstract: Stakeholder theory asks who is in, who is out, and who gets what. Existing work illuminates important dimensions of firm–stakeholder relationships but does not supply a common, transaction-level rule connecting these questions. We use the Coase theorem to develop such a rule. A Coasian stakeholder is an actor with shutdown power, defined as the de facto capacity, within the relevant time horizon, to prevent, materially delay, or substantially reduce the expected joint value of a focal value-creating transaction. If all such actors are identified and bargaining and enforcement are costless, value-maximizing transactions proceed, although rights and bargaining positions may affect who captures value. When transaction costs are positive, however, identification, bargaining, coalition formation, and enforcement can delay, distort, or suppress those transactions. Across six propositions, we explain how shutdown power is identified and acquired, how complementarity and bargaining conditions shape value capture, how firms reshape stakeholder sets through coalition costs and governance design, and why consolidated opposition can sometimes preserve transactions that fragmented claims would suppress.

papers.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
papers.abstract: We study how firms choose among incentive contracts and how accurately managers predict their effects. Using a survey of managerial beliefs and a large-scale field experiment, we randomly assign agents at the market level to several widely used, expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes. In the field, the best-performing contract raises weekly firm profit by over 55% relative to the status quo, despite being ranked lower by managers, whereas the worst-performing contract performs as predicted. Managers reliably avoid poorly performing contracts but systematically underestimate top-performing ones. Standard contract theory does better as a forecaster here: an unbiased textbook principal orders the contracts correctly, or very nearly so, correctly identifying the profit leader where managers do not; where it does miss, the error is similar to managers’ and for a similar reason. We show that the performance differences across contracts reflect a mix of labor-supply and risk responses, and that managerial predictability varies with contract complexity and managerial hierarchy. Our results highlight the importance of contract design for firm performance and reveal systematic limits to managerial cognition in shaping incentives.

papers.title: Global Entrepreneurial Talent Flows: Widely Funded, Selectively Successful?
papers.abstract: Immigrant founders of US venture-backed startups exit successfully more often than native founders. Does this hold worldwide? Using career histories for 913,226 founder-firm pairs in 213 countries (1990–2026), we compare founders who build abroad (expats) or return home after foreign experience (returnees) with comparable local founders in the same country. Both expats and returnees raise early funding more often globally. Expats' success premium, however, concentrates in the US (18 percent) and UK (26 percent), especially among those entering the US through graduate school, work, or direct founding. Returnees rarely show such a premium. Capital follows mobile founders across borders, but success follows them selectively.

papers.title: Selective Admissions in Nursing Homes: Evidence from a Randomized Audit Study
papers.abstract: It has been widely documented that patients in the US who are associated with disadvantaged demographics receive care at lower quality nursing homes. To understand the role that selective admissions may play in contributing to this pattern, we conducted a nationwide audit study of the impact of patient race, payer, and medical condition on responses to about 5,500 availability inquiries sent to about 3,000 nursing homes. We find 10-15% lower availability for Medicaid patients compared to private-pay patients and for patients with Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without; these availability gaps generally increase with nursing home quality. We find no statistically significant evidence of differential availability by race. To quantify the implications of these selective admissions practices, we embed the audit study results in a model of constrained nursing home choice. We estimate that if, counterfactually, Medicaid patients had the same choice sets as their private-pay counterparts, they would attend higher quality nursing homes on average, but the private-Medicaid gap in quality would be reduced by only 5-10%. Our results suggest that supply-side availability differences by payer are widespread, but that they are unlikely to be the primary factor behind the observed gap in quality of nursing homes attended.
